title: Google Paid $10M for a Bankrupt Airline's Data: Data Is the Moat in the AI Era
dek: In the AI era, a company's most valuable asset is its data—Google paid $10 million for a bankrupt airline's data; AI agents with legitimate access are the new biggest threat, and data infrastructure must be rebuilt.
why: Eon's founders turn the 'data moat' from a slogan into a calculable judgment using real cases like bankrupt airline data and a 60% ransomware exposure rate, and offer a new threat model for agent security.
who: CTOs, data platform leads, and AI engineers focused on data assets and security in the AI era, plus investors evaluating data company valuations.
skip: You can skip the cold open; start at 1:27 for the main discussion.

points.h: Models and compute have zero switching costs; only data is uniquely yours
points.body: The Eon founders point out that models and compute have near-zero switching costs, leaving data as the only truly unique asset. Two days ago, Google bought data from bankrupt Spirit Airlines for $10 million, with another bidder reportedly Mercor. This is no longer an isolated case: CEOs are often asked if they'd sell their data, and AI labs even approach hedge funds on Wall Street to buy data. Real enterprise data has become scarce fuel for training agents, and even bankrupt companies' data can become auction items.

points.h: Real enterprise data is scarcer than you think; much public data is synthetic
points.body: The host questions whether 'data is the new oil' held in the slogan era, but post-training and reinforcement learning have turned it into real demand. Companies like Applied Comp offer fine-tuning services on datasets, but Eon argues that truly usable real enterprise datasets are extremely scarce, and much public data is synthetic. Spirit Airlines' data can train airline customer service agents and also serve as a panoramic sample of how a large enterprise operates—hierarchies, middle management, and worker collaboration—exactly the material agent training lacks most.

points.h: Data silos aren't a tool problem; incentives are misaligned
points.body: Data tools are plentiful; the problem is data locked in business units. In the past, data teams chose their own projects and tools (Fivetran, DBT, Monte Carlo). Now CEOs, educated by ChatGPT, demand data activation, but data is scattered across 20-year-old systems, even on servers no one dares to shut down. Extracting data requires engineers and comes at the cost of security, compliance, and production disruptions; business leaders and platform teams have fundamentally misaligned incentives. Eon's approach is to first automatically map, classify, and build a semantic layer, then continuously supply data without impacting production.

points.h: Security models were built for humans; the intruders are now agents
points.body: Existing security models target human threats. At AWS, Eon saw a customer whose environment was 60% exposed to ransomware because resources weren't properly mapped, classified, or tagged. Now the same threat comes from non-human actors—AI agents with legitimate access that can drop a table in an instant. Detection and recovery methodologies are similar, but the speed is extreme. A few months ago, nearly every enterprise customer either feared agent attacks or had already experienced one; organizations must design defenses assuming they are already compromised.

points.h: More agents mean dashboards are more essential, not less
points.body: Enterprise data stacks were built around humans asking questions via dashboards; agents will dynamically reason over larger datasets, access SaaS and historical data, and take direct action. The guests believe dashboards won't disappear—they'll become more common because humans need to understand what agents are doing in the environment. Coding agents will write most code, agents will activate other agents, and tracking non-human identities (NHIs) becomes a core challenge, spawning a wave of NHI security companies. When non-technical employees build agents with Lovable, they don't even know the data compliance boundaries, creating new actors in the organization not bound by rules.

points.h: Legacy pipelines aren't connected because full context wasn't needed before
points.body: Take buying coffee with a card: the transaction is written to a database, extracted, and sent elsewhere for separate processing. Pipelines aren't connected because full context wasn't needed before—you only handled predefined questions. Today, if you can intelligently collect, efficiently store, and activate data, you enable combinatorial insights: merging a list of 'people in New York who like burgers' with 'people in New York who like pizza' yields a new audience. Data ingestion is growing wildly, old ETL tools can't handle multi-party noise, and vendors like Databricks are reinventing themselves.

points.h: AI transformation is faster than cloud, yet customers have less control
points.body: The Eon founders did large-scale cloud migrations at AWS, with customers running from thousands to hundreds of thousands of servers; transformation required both technical and human investment. AI-era transformation is an intensified version of the cloud era, but customers are losing control—fearing system crashes, data leaks, and IP exfiltration—and control has become a restraining factor. Cloud is abstract, but AI is understandable to everyone (the ChatGPT moment), so boards push companies to adopt AI from both 'opportunity' and 'fear' angles. Traditional enterprises needing rapid deployment can only shorten sales cycles by bringing in Silicon Valley engineers with mature solutions and playbooks.

points.h: The fastest AI path for big companies is buying a startup outright
points.body: The way enterprises consume software is changing. Large traditional enterprises want AI but internal processes take one to two years, so they bring in top engineers and ready-made solutions to accelerate; product-led growth (PLG) is particularly effective in AI infrastructure, with Cognition as a case of PLG first, then moving to large customers. Another aggressive approach is to acquire a startup directly and transform it into an AI company, thereby improving margins and efficiency faster. The guests believe 'the revolution has just begun'—most companies are still at the start of their AI journey, but eventually all will be pushed forward.
